summary: Specifies a second version of Robust Header Compression profiles for RTP, UDP, IP, ESP and UDP-Lite headers. It simplifies the rules and adds robustness against loss and reordering. It supersedes the earlier profiles in RFC 3095, RFC 3843 and RFC 4019 without making them obsolete. It is a standards-track specification.

eli5.summary: Packets repeat lots of the same information in their headers. ROHCv2 shortens that repeated part so slow or noisy links carry more useful data.

questions: how does rohc handle packet reordering
what is the rohcv2 decompressor state machine
subtitle: A second generation of header compression profiles that survives packet loss and reordering on slow links.

tldr.problem: Packet headers repeat almost the same values from one packet to the next, which wastes capacity on slow or lossy links, and the first ROHC profiles in RFC 3095 required in-order delivery between compressor and decompressor.
tldr.mechanism: Six ROHCv2 profiles compress RTP, UDP, UDP-Lite, ESP and IP headers by sending changing fields in compressed form protected by CRCs, with a decompressor state machine and feedback that lets the compressor repair a damaged context.
tldr.outcome: ROHCv2 tolerates a limited amount of reordering and simplifies the rules of the earlier profiles. It supersedes the profiles of RFC 3095, RFC 3843 and RFC 4019 but does not obsolete them.

facts.value: 8 least significant bits of the MSN

today: RFC 5225 is a Proposed Standard. It supersedes the profile definitions in RFC 3095, RFC 3843 and RFC 4019 without making them obsolete, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Six Profiles for Header Compression
sections.content:
The ROHC working group built a header compression framework on which profiles can be defined for different protocol sets. The framework was first documented in RFC 3095, with later profiles for IP headers in RFC 3843 and UDP-Lite headers in RFC 4019. RFC 5225 defines an updated version of each of those profiles, and depends on the ROHC framework in RFC 4995, which is required reading.

It defines six profiles, each with a profile identifier: RTP/UDP/IP is 0x0101, UDP/IP is 0x0102, ESP/IP is 0x0103, IP is 0x0104, RTP/UDP-Lite/IP is 0x0107 and UDP-Lite/IP is 0x0108. Each can also compress AH, GRE, MINE, and the IPv6 Destination Options, Hop-by-hop Options and Routing extension headers.
sections.eli5: ROHCv2 is a set of six recipes for shrinking the labels on different kinds of network packets.

sections.title: What Changed From the RFC 3095 Profiles
sections.content:
Most header fields never or seldom change, so they can be compressed away. A few need more care: the IPv4 Identification field, the ESP sequence number, the UDP and UDP-Lite checksums, the UDP-Lite checksum coverage, the RTP marker bit, the RTP sequence number and the RTP timestamp. The RTP timestamp usually correlates strongly with the RTP sequence number, and the IPv4 Identification often correlates with the master sequence number (MSN) used for compression.

ROHCv2 aims for compression efficiency and robustness at least equal to the RFC 3095 profiles under the same conditions. The main differences are these.

  • Reordering: RFC 3095 profiles require in-order delivery between the endpoints. ROHCv2 can handle a limited amount of reordering itself.
  • Operation: RFC 3095 defines several modes. ROHCv2 runs unidirectionally until feedback is first received for a context, then bidirectionally, and the formats do not depend on this.
  • Extension headers and nesting: They are chained like other headers rather than list-compressed, and any number of IP headers can be compressed instead of at most two.
  • Repair and feedback: There is no IR-DYN packet; a compressed header with a 7-bit CRC does the repair. A CRC in FEEDBACK-2 is mandatory.
sections.eli5: The old recipes needed packets to arrive in order. The new ones cope when a few arrive a bit late, and they have fewer special cases to remember.

sections.title: How Compressor and Decompressor Cooperate
sections.content:
The compressor uses an optimistic approach: when a field changes, it keeps sending a header type that carries the new value until it is fairly confident the decompressor has received it. The number of repetitions depends on the loss and reordering of the link and is left to implementers.

When it starts a flow, the compressor sends Initialization and Refresh (IR) packets and does not expect feedback. Once feedback arrives, the flow moves from unidirectional to bidirectional operation, and the compressor can choose smaller headers based on what it knows about the decompressor. Until a feedback channel is established, the compressor SHOULD send IR packets periodically.

Window-based LSB encoding gives a tradeoff: the interpretation interval can cover reordering (negative deltas) or consecutive losses (positive deltas), and widening one narrows the other. Compressors should tune their strategy to the loss and reordering of the link.

The decompressor checks every decompression with a CRC and only then updates its context. It may skip updating the context with a successfully decompressed sequentially late packet, so older data does not overwrite newer.
sections.eli5: The sender keeps repeating a new fact until it is pretty sure the receiver got it. The receiver can shout back if something looks wrong.

sections.title: The Decompressor State Machine
sections.content:
The decompressor has three states. In No Context (NC) it has not yet validated an IR header, so only IR packets can be decompressed. A successful 8-bit CRC check on an IR header takes it to Full Context (FC), where it assumes its whole context is valid and may try any packet type.

When context damage is detected, the decompressor drops to Repair Context (RC), where only IR headers and CO headers with a 7-bit CRC are decompressed. It returns to FC when one of those verifies. If static context damage is assumed, it falls to NC and only IR headers will do.

How damage is detected is left to implementations. On damage the decompressor should send a NACK, and on static damage a STATIC-NACK, subject to a limit on the feedback rate.
sections.eli5: The receiver is either lost, unsure or confident. A good full message makes it confident, and bad-looking messages make it less sure until a good one arrives.

sections.title: Control Fields, Verification and Feedback
sections.content:
Every ROHCv2 header carries a Master Sequence Number (MSN), one space per context. It identifies reference headers in feedback and lets the decompressor infer incrementing fields. For the profiles where the compressor creates it (0x0102, 0x0104 and 0x0108), it starts at a random value and SHOULD go up by one per packet.

Other control fields include the reordering ratio, the IP-ID behavior (sequential, byte-swapped, random or constant zero), the UDP-Lite coverage behavior, the timestamp stride and the time stride. A 3-bit CRC protects the control fields in co_common and co_repair. The default ts_stride is 160 and scaling the RTP timestamp is optional. Timer-based compression is also optional for both sides.

An IR header is checked with an 8-bit CRC and a CO header with a 3-bit or 7-bit CRC. If a check fails, the context MUST NOT be updated, and a packet that cannot be verified MUST NOT be delivered to upper layers. If the channel cannot guarantee in-order delivery, ROHC segmentation MUST NOT be used.

Feedback comes in FEEDBACK-1 (an ACK carrying 8 bits of the MSN) and FEEDBACK-2, which has an Acktype, the acknowledgment number, a CRC and options. Once a decompressor starts feedback for a context, it is REQUIRED to continue for the life of that context.
sections.eli5: Each packet gets a counter so everyone can tell which one is which, and a small check number so a garbled packet is not accepted by mistake.

sections.title: Header Formats and Chains
sections.content:
Compressed headers are described in the ROHC formal notation. ROHCv2 uses two header types: the IR header, which carries the static and dynamic parts of the context, and the CO header, which is compressed. The IR header has an IR type octet (11111101), the profile octet, an 8-bit CRC, then a static chain and a dynamic chain.

Chains group fields by behavior and are built by appending one item per header, starting with the outermost. The static chain appears only in IR. The dynamic chain appears in IR and co_repair. The irregular chain appears in all CO headers except co_repair. Extension headers get all three chains like other headers.

Two sets of CO formats exist, one for a sequential innermost IP-ID and one for the rest, plus shared formats. co_common updates a changed field pattern and carries a 7-bit CRC; co_repair conveys all dynamic fields uncompressed and is useful when context damage is assumed. Each profile has its own variants in the RFC.
sections.eli5: The first message is a full description. After that, short messages carry only what is different, sorted into piles of things that never change, sometimes change and always change.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Bit errors, lost packets and reordering could make a decompressor rebuild packets that do not match the original but still look valid, possibly with valid UDP checksums. The profiles use an internal checksum to make this unlikely; the chance that consecutive erroneous packets go unnoticed is close to zero.

Integrity protection applied after compression does not remove this small remaining probability if an attacker can discard or reorder packets. End-to-end integrity mechanisms are not affected by compression and can catch corruption from a faulty or malicious compressor.

An intruder who injects bogus IR or FEEDBACK packets could reduce compression efficiency, but the RFC notes that the ability to inject arbitrary link-layer packets raises larger security issues.
sections.eli5: A damaged note could be rebuilt wrongly, so each one carries a check number. Someone sneaking fake notes in could slow things down.

sections.title: IANA Profile Identifiers
sections.content: IANA has assigned ROHC profile identifiers to the six profiles: 0x0101 for ROHCv2 RTP, 0x0102 for UDP, 0x0103 for ESP, 0x0104 for IP, 0x0107 for RTP/UDP-Lite and 0x0108 for UDP-Lite.
sections.eli5: Each of the six recipes gets its own number so both ends know which one they are using.
